book.title: Cauda Equina Syndrome (CES)
book.lead: This chapter is mainly about recognition and fast referral. The physiotherapist does not treat CES. The physiotherapist identifies it and sends the patient to hospital without delay.

blocks.text: The **cauda equina** (Latin for horse's tail) is the bundle of nerve roots that runs below the end of the spinal cord, in the lower lumbar canal. These roots supply the legs, the bladder, the bowel, the genital area and the saddle area (inner thighs, buttocks, perineum). **Cauda equina syndrome** happens when these roots are compressed. The most common cause is a large central disc herniation. Other causes include tumour, infection or abscess, bleeding, severe stenosis and trauma [Ref - to verify].

CES is uncommon, but delay can lead to lasting loss of bladder, bowel and sexual function and leg weakness [Ref - to verify]. Because it is uncommon and the symptoms can be subtle, it is easy to miss.
CES is often described in two stages. These are teaching terms, not a replacement for medical assessment.

rows: Low back pain, often with sciatica on one or both sides; altered sensation in the saddle area; changed bladder sensation (for example reduced feeling of needing to pass urine, difficulty starting, weak stream, urgency)
Painless urinary retention with overflow incontinence, loss of bowel control, marked saddle numbness, bilateral leg weakness, sexual dysfunction

blocks.text: The window for best outcome is before the late stage, so any suspicion at the early stage needs action. Do not wait for retention.

sections.title: C. Ask the right questions (every patient with back or leg pain)

rows: Any numbness or pins and needles around the genitals, anus or inner thighs? Is it when you wipe after the toilet?
Has anything changed with passing urine: difficulty starting, weak flow, not feeling it, leaking?
Any change in bowel control, or not feeling when you need to go?
Any change in sexual function or genital sensation?
Leg pain or weakness in both legs? Is it getting worse?
Any recent heavy lifting, trauma, fever, cancer history, injections?

blocks.text: Ask these questions plainly and privately. Patients may feel embarrassed and may not volunteer the information.

sections.title: D. Physical examination (do not delay referral to complete it)

items: Gait and heel and toe walking.
Myotomes L2 to S1 on both sides; ankle plantar flexion and big toe movements are key.
Dermatomes L1 to S1 on both sides.
Reflexes: patellar and Achilles, both sides.

**Saddle sensation:** only if trained and permitted by local scope, with clear explanation, consent and a chaperone. Compare light touch and pinprick around the anal area and genital area with the thigh. Do not perform internal rectal examination unless it is within your role and training.
Check the clinical picture, vital signs and general state.

blocks.text: **Rule:** if the history is highly suggestive, send the patient to hospital now. A normal examination does not clear a patient who reports saddle numbness or bladder change.

There is no single physiotherapy special test that confirms CES. The diagnosis is made in hospital, usually by urgent MRI together with clinical assessment and bladder checks (for example bladder scan) [Ref - to verify]. The physiotherapist's tools are:

rows: Identify the pattern that needs emergency imaging
Saddle sensation change, bladder or bowel change, bilateral neurological signs, progression
Any one of the symptoms in section B reported by the patient, or objective saddle sensory loss
No such symptoms and normal neurological exam. This lowers concern but does not remove the need to re-ask at every visit
A symptom screen is not a diagnosis. Many people with these screening symptoms do not have CES, but the cost of missing it is high
One leg, no bladder or saddle symptoms
Urinary tract infection or prostate problem
Burning urine, frequency, no saddle numbness, normal neurology
Ask about urine symptoms, back pain
Medical review. If neurology is abnormal, treat as CES until excluded
Both upper motor and lower motor signs, earlier bladder signs
Do not assume. Exclude CES first

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Stop treatment; send to emergency department the same day, state suspected CES clearly
New sexual dysfunction with back pain
Bilateral or rapidly progressive leg weakness

blocks.text: Call ahead to the hospital if possible. Document the time, findings and who was informed. Ask someone to accompany the patient. Do not allow the patient to drive. Do not delay for a scan request, a second opinion or a night of observation.
**Stop:** all treatment, including manual therapy, exercise and traction.

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Does the patient report any of: saddle numbness, new bladder or bowel change, new sexual dysfunction, or bilateral progressive leg symptoms? **Yes:** emergency referral now.
**No:** continue the relevant pathway and re-screen at every visit.
If unsure: refer, and explain the reason in the referral note.

sections.title: I to K. Manual therapy, exercise and modalities

blocks.text: Not applicable before diagnosis and surgical review. Do not apply them to a patient with suspected CES. After surgery, treatment follows the surgeon's instruction (see L).

items: **Recognise and refer** (this section G).

**Hospital phase:** usually urgent imaging and a decision about decompression surgery by the medical team. Earlier decompression is generally associated with better outcomes, but exact timing guidance varies [Ref - to verify].
**Rehabilitation after surgery or conservative medical care:** a team approach including a physician, nurse, continence specialist, pelvic health physiotherapist and occupational therapist.

**Physiotherapy goals:** safe walking, strength recovery for the affected muscles, balance, falls prevention, pain management, education about bladder and bowel routines (guided by the specialist team), pelvic floor referral, and return to function.
**Long-term support:** some patients keep bladder, bowel, sexual or pain problems. Psychological support and peer information are important.

blocks.text: If you are rehabilitating a patient after CES, track muscle strength, gait, balance, sensation, pain, bladder and bowel function (using the specialist team's tools) and participation. Any new deterioration means urgent medical review.

**Case:** A 34-year-old woman has 5 days of low back pain and right leg pain. She mentions that urine has been harder to start for 2 days and she did not feel the toilet paper when wiping. Left leg feels heavy. Reflexes appear slightly reduced at the ankles. She says it is probably stress.
**Decision:** suspected CES. Stop the session, explain the concern simply, arrange emergency hospital transfer the same day, give the clinician a written summary, and document time and actions.

items: The patient can still pass urine. Is CES excluded? No. CES can start with altered sensation and difficulty starting or weak flow before retention occurs. The early stage is the best time to act.
Why not wait one day to see whether symptoms settle? Delay is linked to worse outcomes and the damage may be permanent [Ref - to verify].
The patient is embarrassed and asks you not to refer. What do you do? Explain calmly why it is important, check that they understand, and refer. Respect their feelings, but the safety risk is high.
Why ask about bladder and saddle symptoms every time, not only on the first visit? CES can develop after the first assessment, for example after a disc herniation enlarges.
Normal reflexes and strong legs but saddle numbness. What now? Emergency referral. Saddle numbness alone is enough reason to act.
**Initial approach:** recognise and refer the same day.
**Justifying findings:** saddle sensory change, bladder, bowel or sexual change, bilateral progressive signs.
**Priority:** speed and clear communication.
**Manual therapy, exercise, modalities:** none until medical clearance.
**Tell the patient:** you need urgent hospital assessment today; this is not a routine back problem.
**Avoid:** waiting, reassuring without checking, driving.
**Measure after recovery:** function, strength, bladder and bowel status.
**If symptoms are doubtful:** refer anyway.
**Discharge:** only after specialist rehabilitation goals are met.
**Can be tested:** which symptom combinations best predict MRI-confirmed compression; how timing relates to outcome.
**Hypotheses:** that early recognition by physiotherapists improves outcomes (plausible but needs confirmation).
**Future questions:** safest minimum screening tool for primary care physiotherapy.

blocks.text: Evidence not graded until references are verified.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Explain what the cauda equina is and why compression is serious.
Ask the screening questions clearly and sensitively.
State the action and urgency when a screening symptom is positive.
Write a short referral that says suspected cauda equina syndrome.

sections.A: Cauda equina spinal cord ke neeche nerve roots ka guchha hai jo taangon, peshab, pakhane aur jinsi kaam ko control karta hai. In par dabao emergency hai.
sections.B: Shuru mein kamar dard, sciatica aur peshab ki halki tabdeeli; baad mein peshab ruk jana ya nikal jana. Jaldi pehchanna zaroori hai.
sections.C: Har kamar ya taang dard ke patient se saaf aur izzat se poochein: saddle area mein sunn-pan, peshab, pakhane ya jinsi kaam mein tabdeeli.
sections.D: Chaal, dono taangon ki taaqat, sensation aur reflexes. Lekin exam poora karne ke liye referral mein der na karein.
sections.E: Koi physio test CES confirm nahi karta. Diagnosis hospital mein MRI se hota hai.
sections.F: Ek taraf ka sciatica, peshab ka infection ya prostate ka masla isi jaisa lag sakta hai.
sections.G: Saddle sunn-pan, peshab ya pakhane ki nayi tabdeeli, nayi jinsi takleef, ya dono taangon mein barhte symptoms: abhi emergency referral.
sections.H: Agar in mein se koi bhi symptom ho to foran emergency referral. Intezaar nahi.
sections.I: Diagnosis aur surgery ke faisle se pehle koi manual therapy, exercise ya machine nahi.
sections.L: Pehchanein aur refer karein. Hospital mein jaldi MRI aur surgery ka faisla hota hai. Surgery ke baad rehab surgeon ki hidayat par.
sections.M: Surgery ke baad taaqat, chaal, balance, sensation aur peshab-pakhane ka haal track karein.
sections.N: 34 saal ki khatoon ko peshab shuru karne mein mushkil aur saddle mein sunn-pan hai. Khud socho kya karna hai, phir jawab dekho.
sections.chapter-summary-decision: Mukhtasar: pehchano aur usi din refer karo.
